newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Takeover seen as only answer to S.Korea Kia's woes.
newsitem.headline: Takeover seen as only answer to S.Korea Kia's woes.

text.p: A plan by South Korea's embattled Kia Group to cut affiliates, sell assets and trim its workforce was little more than a bandage treatment, analysts said on Wednesday.
At most, they said, South Korea's eighth biggest conglomerate would be patched up well enough to last through December presidential elections.
Another big corporate collapse before the vote would be politically unacceptable, the analysts said.
In the end, the most likely scenario was for Kia to be broken up and sold off other conglomerates, with its carmaking division going to Samsung Motors, the analysts said.
"Even if Kia cuts itself down to just Kia Motors and Asia Motors, the way forward is still pretty murky," said Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K.) Ltd.
"It will still be saddled with the same super competitive domestic market and a very competitive global market."
Slumping sales at home, exacerbated by the resurgence of rival Daewoo Motor, had crippled flagship Kia Motors, the group's cash cow, the analysts said.
An unofficial bank committee stepped in on Tuesday to rescue Kia from imminent failure, selecting 18 of Kia's 38 global affiliates for bail-out.
"There is no way to rescue Kia," said Lee Jung-ja, head of research at HSBC James Capel.
"The problem with selling off Kia Steel or Asia Motors is that there is already oversupply in those industries."
Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities, said any break-up and sale of Kia would come after the elections.
"Other chaebols would be very interested in taking Kia over, but the government won't do anything until after the election to avoid criticism," he said.
Unlike South Korea's other conglomerates, known as "chaebol", Kia is not owned by a single family or individual.
"They have that aura of little guy battling against the giants. There is a lot of sympathy in certain quarters with that," said Coryo's Morris.

Analysts said Ford Motor was the largest single shareholder of Kia Motors with a stake estimated at between 16.9 and 20 percent, followed by Hyundai Motor with 9.4 percent and Samsung Group with 6.3 percent.
Once the election was over, analysts said the government was likely to set aside concerns about the increasing power and influence of chaebols and allow a healthy group to acquire Kia.
State-run Korea Development Bank is Kia's largest creditor, which makes the government the key decision-maker.

"They will say selling the company can solve potential oversupply in the auto industry and reduce pressure on the banking sector. Probably resistance will be weak because people will realise the great impact of Kia's failure," Lee said.
Samsung was considered the most likely group to take over Kia because of its own automaking aspirations and its financial resources.
Rumours that Samsung was interested in Kia as a short-cut into the industry's top ranks have been swirling for months.
The contrarian view was that the government would override social concerns and push for an immediate takeover.
"The government will want to solve this problem as soon as possible. It has to be resolved before the election," said James Son, auto analyst at SBC Warburg Securities.
Son said allowing the Kia situation to drag into next year could lead to many bankruptcies among Kia Motors' estimated 5,000 subcontractors and hurt Korean financial institutions in overseas markets.
